[empty-drift-snapshot-fails-ci] Defect · A committed drift snapshot with zero rules fails CI, and okl verify never creates the first one
symptom: a new user commits okl-drift.json on day one, before any lesson has --files, and the okl-verify CI step fails with 'NOTHING CHECKED' (exit 2); or a user verifies a lesson and finds no okl-drift.json to commit
fix: commit okl-drift.json only once a lesson governs files: run okl export --drift once, then let okl verify refresh it; documented in the Quickstart. Candidate code fix: have export --drift refuse (exit 2) to write a snapshot with zero rules, so the trap cannot be set
body: cause: the CI workflow treats exit 2 from 'okl drift --gate --snapshot' as broken whenever a snapshot is present, because a configured store that checked nothing usually means an outage. An empty snapshot is indistinguishable from that. Separately, okl verify only refreshes an okl-drift.json that already exists (by design: never created as a side effect), so the first one must come from okl export --drift. The README told users to commit the snapshot unconditionally until #69; found 2026-09-27 by running a zero-rule snapshot through the gate.

[n_805cf67e5cc5] Defect · Drift misses a change committed within the same second as a verification
symptom: a file edited and committed immediately after okl verify does not show as drift
fix: record the commit the check passed at and compare the governed files' CONTENT there with HEAD (git diff --quiet <commit> HEAD -- <paths>); fall back to time only when the clone lacks the commit; bind the commit into tamper-evident evidence; test with a pinned same-second commit date, never a sleep
body: cause: drift compares git's last commit time for the governed files against the rule's verified_at. Git stores commit time to the second; verified_at is in milliseconds. A commit in the same second as the stamp is floored to the start of that second and so compares as BEFORE a stamp taken later in it. Found while writing the #21 regression test, which verified then committed within one second and saw no drift. Rare by hand, plausible in a script that runs okl verify then commits. The same comparison also trusted each commit's clock, so a commit from a machine running ahead read as a change the check never saw. Fixed in #107 (issue #102): okl verify records the commit the check passed at, and drift diffs the governed files there against HEAD; the commit is bound into the evidence ahead of the time stamp so a committed snapshot cannot clear it by hand, and time is only the fallback when a clone lacks that commit.

[n_5ddb0776a863] Defect · A CI gate that reads gitignored state checks nothing in CI, and passes
symptom: a gate is green on every PR and never red, and the data it inspects lives in a file the repository ignores
fix: make the gate count what it inspected and treat zero as 'did not run' (its own exit code), never as clean; then decide explicitly how CI gets the data, rather than letting its absence read as success. The same holds for any report or summary line that states a clean result: carry the inspected count beside it and say 'unknown' at zero (okl recap --report printed 'every lesson is proven' with drift having checked nothing, caught in review on okl #281, 2026-10-24)
body: cause: okl drift --gate reads the knowledge store, and okl init gitignores the store because it holds machine-local paths and credentials. CI therefore never had one. Reading the unconfigured directory silently created an empty okl.db, found no rules in it, and printed 'OK - no encoded rule's governed source changed'. On the same commit a developer's local store showed 45 drifted rules. The gate was made a required branch check before this was noticed, which is what made it urgent: a required green that proved nothing. The renderer's own docstring warned that 'no output and the check did not run look identical, and only one of them is safe' - and then printed the all-clear for the not-run case. Fixed by refusing the unconfigured read, counting checked rules, returning 2 under --gate when zero were checked, and having the shipped workflow surface that as a warning annotation instead of a pass.

[doc-claim-governs-doc-and-code] Rule · Wire a doc claim to a check that governs the doc AND the code it describes
symptom: a README or guide states a command, flag, default or number that the code stopped supporting, and nothing went red
fix: record the claim as a Rule with --files naming both the doc and the code it depends on; verify with a check that fails if they disagree (run the documented command; compare the documented default with the code's); normalise whitespace when matching prose, because doc lines wrap; prove the check red by breaking one side on purpose
body: cause: docs drift in exactly the gap between checks. A drift rule on README.md alone re-opens when prose changes but not when the code under the claim moves; a check that only greps the doc for expected words passes forever. Found 2026-09-29: a docs audit of a repo that dogfoods its own drift tool found ~74 stale claims, because only one README rule existed and it checked positioning, not facts.

[n_b0457b37c65a] Decision · A controlled vocabulary is closed per store, not fixed in the package
symptom: a validated vocabulary ships as a constant, so a team using a language or subject the authors did not anticipate must fork to file a lesson
fix: keep the shipped set as a FLOOR and let the store declare additions as records; validate against floor union declared, and validate the declaration itself against the floor only so the first one is writable
body: cause: KNOWN_TAGS was the entire vocabulary. A language-support audit drove a Rust repo end to end - init, record, check, drift, verify all worked, because drift asks git about path globs and verification runs whatever command it is given - and the single failure was 'okl record --tags rust', whose only remedy was forking. The point of a closed vocabulary is catching the typo that files a record where nobody looks, and closed-per-store keeps that: rustt is still refused in a store that declared rust. What changes is who may grow it. Deliberately NOT extended: the stack list gating applies_to, because 4h measured that filter changing 0 percent of delivered slots, and extending an exclusive mechanism without a measurement is the 4d defect.

[n_b4050b826687] Defect · A verification stamp earned by grepping for expected strings proves nothing about what else is there
symptom: a verify --run that greps for text the artifact is expected to contain
fix: assert the absence of the bad state, not the presence of the good one: enumerate what the artifact claims and require each claim to resolve to committed evidence
body: cause: the check asked 'do these strings appear?' The risk was the opposite question — 'does an unsupported claim appear?' The diagram passed its drift stamp for weeks while publishing figures the report itself quarantines as historical, on a public page whose prose cited the receipted numbers beside them.

[n_31bde92d9003] Rule · Verification stamps come from observed checks with stored evidence — never from the claimant's assertion
symptom: a 'verified' flag settable by whoever makes the claim, with no record of what check (if any) backed it
fix: no run, no stamp: verification API takes evidence produced by an executed check; keep assertion-based flags only for importing historical receipts
body: cause: assertion-based verification is a step grading itself — the flag carries the recorder's confidence, not evidence, and nothing distinguishes 'tested' from 'believed'. The mechanism: a verify operation that (1) runs the named check itself and reads the real outcome, (2) optionally requires a positive success signal in the output so exit-0 alone can't certify, (3) stores the command + result + timestamp as an evidence trail on the record, making every stamp inspectable and re-runnable by anyone later. Full independence then comes from the outer layers re-running the evidence: CI on every PR, drift when governed files change, TTL decay.

[n_58119d0a63d9] Rule · Init must wire, not instruct — every 'now copy X / add Y to config' printout is a surface nobody runs
symptom: an installer prints manual follow-up steps (register this hook, copy this workflow, add to settings)
fix: make init perform each registration itself, idempotent and non-clobbering; warn loudly only for what it truly cannot do (e.g. no git repo -> drift disabled)
body: cause: the installer stops where the mechanical work gets fiddly (JSON merging, no-clobber checks), so the last mile becomes a printed TODO — and the component it gates (hooks, CI verifier, MCP tools) silently never runs. okl init had four of these at once: hooks installed but unregistered in settings.json, a CI workflow that was a copy instruction, verify steps that were echo placeholders, and an MCP registration hint. The fix is always the same shape: do the merge idempotently (preserve existing config, never duplicate, never clobber), and reserve printed output for genuinely human decisions.

[n_e7988ff536fb] Rule · Exit codes are this CLI's public API: 0 clean, 1 findings, 2 refused
symptom: a new command, or a new error path in an existing one, that returns 0 or 1 on a condition meaning 'this did not run'
fix: return 2 and print the reason to stderr; add a test asserting the code and that stdout stayed empty
body: cause: okl runs inside other people's hooks and CI, where the exit code is the only thing read. 0 means the check ran and found nothing; 1 means it ran and found something (drift, duplicates); 2 means it could not run at all — unconfigured, unreachable, rejected credentials, invalid input. Collapsing 2 into 0 is the silence-as-safety failure the whole tool exists to prevent, and collapsing it into 1 makes a misconfiguration look like a finding.

[n_119528a07fa5] Defect · A subprocess test inherits the developer's state; the same test on a clean checkout hits a precondition
symptom: a test passes locally and fails in CI on an exit code from a guard that never fires on a machine that already has the data
fix: test the unit that was untested, not the pipeline around it; when a subprocess needs data the repo does not commit, either supply it in the test or call the function directly
body: cause: the report-time formatter was reachable only through a full harness run, so a test was written to invoke one. On a developer machine it ran; on a clean checkout the harness refuses at pre-flight with exit 5, because the local store is gitignored and no committed data satisfies the retrieval check. The test asserted the exit code was 0 or 1 and CI returned 5. Two mistakes stacked: asserting an exit code that was never the contract, and reaching the target through six minutes of preconditions instead of calling it. Extracting the formatter into drift_banner() made the untested thing testable in one line, with no environment at all. This is the second time in one session that a test was written against ambient state - the first was a regression test that passed against the broken implementation for the same reason.

[seed:dotnet-defects:nc_idor] Defect · Missing ownership scope check is an IDOR (CWE-639) and slips through tests-by-omission
symptom: an endpoint fetches an entity by id with no owner/tenant predicate
fix: add the caller's owner id to the WHERE clause; return 404 (not 403) on no match
body: A resource endpoint that doesn't scope by the caller's identity leaks other users' data. Portable fix: push the ownership predicate INTO the query (read handlers) or check on the tracked entity (write handlers), return 404 not 403 (403 leaks existence). Require an integration test asserting user X cannot read user Y's resource for every scoped-entity endpoint.

[n_849a5b0425ef] Defect · A tag that records where a lesson was FOUND cannot be filtered on as though it recorded where it APPLIES
symptom: a filter treating a provenance label as a scoping predicate; briefings getting shorter and a known-covered task starting to fail
fix: revert to any-match; record applicability separately from provenance before trying again, and measure any retrieval change with the A/B before believing it
body: cause: stack tags (dotnet, geospatial, react) are assigned at import from the repo a lesson came out of. Reading them as applicability and excluding off-stack records hid 35 of 172 org records from a repo that shared their subject — an IDOR rule, 'exit 0 having written zero files', a transposed-coordinates data defect, none of which are about the stack they are tagged with. The briefed arm then reproduced the defect described by a dropped rule, on a task where the baseline reproduced none.

[n_69f673496137] Rule · Verify-by-making-it-fail applies to throwaway diagnostics, not just committed tests
symptom: an ad-hoc shell or one-off script check reports a clean result across every input, and the clean result is the check silently not working
fix: before believing a negative from a hand-rolled check, run it against a case known to be positive; if it cannot produce the failure it screens for, it is not evidence — and note that a no-match grep exits non-zero, so '|| echo 0' converts a broken check into a reassuring one. The same holds in reverse: before believing a positive, run the check against a case known to be negative. A background watcher reported two PRs as reviewed when the bot had only rate-limited them, because an empty jq result passed through tr '\n' ' ' became a single space and [ -n "$x" ] read it as text (okl #280/#281, 2026-10-24). Count results (jq length) and compare numbers, never test captured text for emptiness
body: cause: surveying six pull requests for merge conflicts, a loop ran 'git merge-tree --write-tree main branch' and grepped the output for CONFLICT, falling back to '|| echo 0'. All six reported zero conflicts. Attempting the first merge for real hit a content conflict immediately. Two compounding errors: merge-tree does not report conflicts in the form that was grepped, and the '|| echo 0' fallback turned grep's no-match exit status into a printed zero, so a broken check and a clean repo were indistinguishable. The discipline was applied rigorously to every committed test that session - each one proved red by injected breakage before being trusted - and skipped for the one-off diagnostic, which was the one that lied. A throwaway check gets believed exactly as much as a test does, so it has to earn it the same way: point it at a case that must fail and confirm it says so.

[seed:dotnet-canon:r_authz_test_required] Rule · Authorization behavior is only proven by an authorization-FAILURE test — clean builds and passing unit tests say nothing
symptom: a scoped-entity endpoint shipped without a cross-user access-denied test
fix: add the X-cannot-read-Y integration test asserting 404 with every scoped endpoint
body: Every endpoint returning or mutating a scoped entity requires an integration test that authenticates as user X, requests user Y's resource, and asserts 404 (not 200, not 403). The absence of exactly this test is how the original IDOR survived undetected for the lifetime of the codebase.

[n_aa3e45a2ecd6] Rule · Provenance references rot precisely because nothing reads them — validate them at startup
symptom: an identifier stored as provenance that no code path dereferences
fix: resolve every such reference at startup and refuse to run on a miss; a field nothing reads is a field nothing checks
files: evals/ab_harness.py,evals/tasks.jsonl
body: cause: each eval task cites the defect_node it tests. The judge uses a separate text signal, so the id is never dereferenced during a run and a typo survives indefinitely — 'r_pin_gating_tool' sat in eight committed receipts while the record was 'r_pin_gating_tools'. The results could not be traced to the lesson they tested, which is the one thing that reference exists to permit.

[n_5ddb0776a863] Defect · A CI gate that reads gitignored state checks nothing in CI, and passes
symptom: a gate is green on every PR and never red, and the data it inspects lives in a file the repository ignores
fix: make the gate count what it inspected and treat zero as 'did not run' (its own exit code), never as clean; then decide explicitly how CI gets the data, rather than letting its absence read as success. The same holds for any report or summary line that states a clean result: carry the inspected count beside it and say 'unknown' at zero (okl recap --report printed 'every lesson is proven' with drift having checked nothing, caught in review on okl #281, 2026-10-24)
body: cause: okl drift --gate reads the knowledge store, and okl init gitignores the store because it holds machine-local paths and credentials. CI therefore never had one. Reading the unconfigured directory silently created an empty okl.db, found no rules in it, and printed 'OK - no encoded rule's governed source changed'. On the same commit a developer's local store showed 45 drifted rules. The gate was made a required branch check before this was noticed, which is what made it urgent: a required green that proved nothing. The renderer's own docstring warned that 'no output and the check did not run look identical, and only one of them is safe' - and then printed the all-clear for the not-run case. Fixed by refusing the unconfigured read, counting checked rules, returning 2 under --gate when zero were checked, and having the shipped workflow surface that as a warning annotation instead of a pass.

[n_fe26d1897041] Defect · A guard that compares against the latest sample fires on the run that repairs the series
symptom: a continuity/regression guard warns on a run that returned to the documented configuration, because the run before it was the anomaly
fix: compare against the MODAL value across the whole history, never the most recent one; and build the discriminating history in the test, because real data stops discriminating the moment the series is repaired
body: cause: a guard added to catch an unnoticed judge swap compared the current run's instrument to the most recent receipt. On its first live run - the run that switched back to the documented judge - the previous receipt was the anomaly itself, so the guard reported NOT COMPARABLE for the run that had just restored comparability. Technically true, practically backwards: it tells the reader to discard the repair, which trains people to ignore the guard. The regression test had the same flaw one level up: it read this repo's real receipts, and once the series is restored the newest receipt IS the modal one, so both implementations agree and the test passed against the broken code. A test that depends on ambient state cannot discriminate the case it exists to discriminate.

[seed:python-canon:py_protocol_isinstance_names_only] Rule · isinstance() against a Protocol checks names, not signatures: conformance comes from the type checker and a shared test
symptom: an isinstance() check against a Protocol, or a Pydantic field typed with one, treated as proof that an implementation fits
fix: type-check the code that wires implementations in; run one shared behaviour test over every implementation; trust isinstance on a Protocol for what it checks, that the members exist, and never as proof of signatures, types or behaviour
body: The Python docs: @runtime_checkable 'will check only the presence of the required methods or attributes, not their type signatures or types.' mypy's docs say the same ('signatures of methods are not checked'), and PEP 544 likens the check to a hasattr() per member. Pydantic inherits the gap: with arbitrary_types_allowed, a field typed with a Protocol is validated by 'a simple check of instance type', and 'nothing in the instance of the arbitrary type is checked'. Reproduced on a published example that offered @runtime_checkable plus a Pydantic model as an extra safety layer: an invoke(a, b, c, d) that returns 42 passed both, and a LangChain chat model passed both, then answered with an AIMessage where the Protocol promised str. The type checker rejected both, and also caught the example's own pipeline passing a PromptValue where its Protocol took str. So a runtime check says an object has the right names, never that it fits. What makes an implementation fit is the type checker over the code that wires it in, plus one behaviour test that every implementation, real or fake, runs.

[eval-scripts-no-exposure] Rule · Every caller of Client.check that briefs no agent asks for it unlogged
symptom: okl metric's exposure counts jump after an eval, a pre-flight or an okl intake run: briefing rows logged for lessons no agent was shown
fix: pass log=False to Client.check (okl intake does; the service honours it as the check request's log field), or set OKL_BRIEFING_LOG=0 before building the Client in an eval or pre-flight script; test it by running the caller against a throwaway store and asserting no briefing row was written
body: cause: Client.check logs each local briefing as exposure (client.py, core.record_briefing). ab_harness.py switched it off, but evals/layout_preflight.py did not, and one run wrote 8 false rows into the real store on 2026-10-10. A new eval script that copies the Client call pattern inherits the same leak; preflight.py is safe only because it calls core.check directly.

[n_dc7429065f5d] Defect · check returns nearly the whole store as 'relevant' — ranking works, filtering doesn't
symptom: a specific task's briefing lists 80%+ of all nodes in scope as relevant
fix: add a relevance cutoff (rank score threshold or top-k) so the briefing stays short; measure against the ADR's miss-rate trigger before tightening
body: cause: FTS matching is permissive enough that a task description matches almost every node. NARROWED 2026-07-21: subject tags + repo-declared interests now filter org nodes by topic (28/33 -> 20/33 on the reference task; remaining hits share a declared interest). Still open: no rank-score cutoff or top-k on the briefing itself.

[n_9ba48d85ed19] Gate · Pre-flight the retrieval before spending on an eval — it is deterministic and answers in milliseconds
symptom: an eval result read as a regression, with no check that each case still receives the input it is testing
fix: run a pre-flight asserting every case's governing record is present in the retrieval it will be given; refuse the run on an unexpected miss; keep known gaps in a named register with reasons, never silent
files: evals/preflight.py,evals/ab_harness.py
body: cause: two separate retrieval regressions were discovered only after full A/B runs (25 minutes, 48 model calls each): a tag-filter change that removed a task's governing rule, and a top-k cutoff that had been dropping another task's rule since it landed. Whether a record reaches a briefing needs no model — it is a deterministic query, and asking it first would have caught both for free.

[n_b578addf6269] Defect · An experiment cannot measure a filter it disables — twice, for two different reasons
symptom: an A/B is run to measure a retrieval change, and the harness's own settings mean the change never affects the briefings it generates
fix: before spending a run on a retrieval change, assert deterministically that the change alters the briefing THIS harness will fetch, with the exact flags it uses; retrieval predicates are answered by a query, not by model calls
body: cause: two consecutive pre-registered runs were framed as measuring applies_to and neither could. The first (REPORT 4e) because no record set the field - it was declared on 7 records that did not exist, and the seed corpus carried the string zero times. The second (4f) because the harness fetches with --interests '', and the filter reads 'if applies and wanted and not (applies & wanted)' - an empty wanted short-circuits it, so a populated field still changes nothing. Both were invisible in the outcome numbers, which looked healthy and inside the noise band. Both took one deterministic query to expose. The pre-flight added after 4b checks that each task's governing RECORD is retrievable; it does not check that a CHANGE UNDER TEST is active in the retrieval path, which is a different question.

[n_041a066035b2] Rule · applies_to stays opt-in: revisit only when off-stack share or framework-bound share roughly doubles
symptom: someone proposes backfilling applies_to across the whole corpus, or asks whether the field is pulling its weight
fix: keep it unset by default and set it only per-record at record time; re-measure the two shares before changing the policy, and never derive the value from a tag
body: cause: measured 2026-09-03 on a 207-record corpus. A python repo's 12 briefing slots were 68 percent untagged/portable, 25 percent off-stack dotnet, 5 percent own-stack, 2 percent off-stack react - and the 32 applies_to-gated records appeared NOWHERE in its ranked candidates, so gating freed zero slots. The off-stack records that do win slots are portable ones (IDOR, pagination caps, rate limiting) that are correctly left unset. Corpus growth alone does not change this: BM25 ranks by match quality, so adding records pushes off-stack ones further down, not up. The scaling risk is the number of distinct STACKS, not corpus size - and its first symptom is redundancy (five stacks each contributing their own pagination rule), which okl dedup addresses, not applicability. Cost asymmetry decides the default: a wrong 'stack-bound' hides a lesson silently, a wrong 'unset' costs one slot of noise. Triggers to revisit: off-stack share of briefings (27 percent at measurement) and framework-bound share of corpus (32/207, 15 percent). Both are queries.

[filter-after-fetch-widens-window] Defect · Filtering results after a fixed-size fetch shrinks the window: widen the fetch by what was dropped
symptom: after some records start being excluded (retired, hidden, filtered), a small top-k returns fewer results or none, and the briefing says nothing matched although a live match ranks just below
fix: re-fetch with the window widened by the number excluded (bounded retries), or filter inside the query; test a small limit with excluded records ranked above a live one
body: cause: okl R2 dropped superseded and obsolete lessons after store.search fetched 3x limit; three obsolete matches above a live one left a limit-1 briefing empty, reading 'no encoded rule matched'.

[n_b83c550a0ca4] Decision · okl stores lessons as typed records found by full-text search, not an ontology store; RDF is a one-way export when something needs it
symptom: a proposal to ingest an ontology, store lessons as RDF triples, or query them with SPARQL or a graph database
fix: keep records, FTS and one-step relationships; when a consumer needs RDF, add a one-way JSON-LD export (never imported back, tested with a real RDF parser); revisit only on a consumer, on exposure-log or A/B misses that cluster around same-concept-different-words (try a measured term map first), or if the job becomes reasoning over a shared concept hierarchy
body: Decided 2026-10-05, recorded in docs/decisions/2026-10-05-records-not-an-ontology-store.md. okl's question is ranked free text (a task sentence, the few lessons that matter, best first) inside a prompt hook in about 0.1s with nothing extra installed; SPARQL has no relevance ranking and stores that rank text bolt on Lucene or Elasticsearch. okl already holds a small ontology (10 record types, 9 one-step relationships, a closed tag vocabulary). Strict classification measured worse here (REPORT 4d: exclusive stack tags hid 35 of 172 records and the briefed arm reproduced the hidden rule's defect), and okl's structural questions are one-line SQL.

[n_849a5b0425ef] Defect · A tag that records where a lesson was FOUND cannot be filtered on as though it recorded where it APPLIES
symptom: a filter treating a provenance label as a scoping predicate; briefings getting shorter and a known-covered task starting to fail
fix: revert to any-match; record applicability separately from provenance before trying again, and measure any retrieval change with the A/B before believing it
body: cause: stack tags (dotnet, geospatial, react) are assigned at import from the repo a lesson came out of. Reading them as applicability and excluding off-stack records hid 35 of 172 org records from a repo that shared their subject — an IDOR rule, 'exit 0 having written zero files', a transposed-coordinates data defect, none of which are about the stack they are tagged with. The briefed arm then reproduced the defect described by a dropped rule, on a task where the baseline reproduced none.

[n_a7634ef53a8f] Decision · The encoding loop has no runtime input — every lesson enters from author time or CI time
symptom: a defect class that only a running system reveals (pagination silently dropped, a limit hit under real load, a partial-failure path) has no way into the store until a human finds it some other way
fix: treat observability as a SOURCE of records rather than a competitor to them: when a runtime-only defect is found, record it with found_by naming the trace or metric that showed it; do not claim the loop covers runtime until some record actually cites one
body: cause: measured 2026-09-23 against the corpus. Of the records that state a found_by, the sources are imported canon (CLAUDE.md sections, dated audits), local reproduction (curl against a running service, a scripted agent call), code review, and tests/CI. None cites telemetry from a deployed system. Classified by keyword and then eyeballed, so treat the buckets as indicative rather than exact - but the absence is not marginal, it is total. This matters because the loop's claim is that a lesson paid for once protects every later task, and it is silent about the class of defect that neither a test nor a review can catch. A vendor post (Milan Jovanovic / Dynatrace, brand partnership) makes the same diagnosis from the other side: its Rule 1, give the agent your production standards up front as a skill rather than a prompt, is this project's thesis implemented as the static per-repo rules file the README already positions against; its Rule 2, make checking runtime data a required step, is an input this project does not have. The two compose - observe discovers, okl encodes, the briefing delivers - and reading it as competition would miss that.

[seed:rag-defects:qz_judge_self] Defect · The LLM judge was grading its own homework (same model as the generator)
symptom: the eval's judge model equals (or defaults to) the generator model
fix: require judge≠generator; refuse to run if they're equal
body: The judge defaulted to the same model as the generator — a mirror, not a signal (its default was even an embedding model that can't generate). Portable rule: the judge must be a different model from the generator; refuse to run if they're equal.

[n_aa3e45a2ecd6] Rule · Provenance references rot precisely because nothing reads them — validate them at startup
symptom: an identifier stored as provenance that no code path dereferences
fix: resolve every such reference at startup and refuse to run on a miss; a field nothing reads is a field nothing checks
files: evals/ab_harness.py,evals/tasks.jsonl

The judge uses a separate text signal, so the id is never dereferenced during a run and a typo survives indefinitely — 'r_pin_gating_tool' sat in eight committed receipts while the record was 'r_pin_gating_tools'. [n_ed7e782d12fd] Defect · Gating writes but not reads leaks the whole store through the dump endpoint
symptom: an auth helper called only from POST handlers, or a token described as gating writes
fix: apply the credential to every route, exempting only a health probe that returns no record content
body: cause: the natural-looking split is that writes need a credential and reads do not. But a knowledge service's reads ARE the sensitive side: GET /nodes returned every record — known defects, retired identifiers, architecture decisions — to any unauthenticated caller.

[n_fe26d1897041] Defect · A guard that compares against the latest sample fires on the run that repairs the series

fix: compare against the MODAL value across the whole history, never the most recent one; and build the discriminating history in the test, because real data stops discriminating the moment the series is repaired

A test that depends on ambient state cannot discriminate the case it exists to discriminate.

[n_0aefd5072428] Claim · Audit verdict: 'Loop Engineering' (B.K. Pandey) — sound taxonomy, exhortation-level; misses cross-run learning and enforcement
body: The 7-block loop framework (goal contract, state, planner, tool allowlist, verifier, recovery, stop rules) is fully covered by existing receipted nodes (qz_agent_contract, qz_broken_tool, r_experiment_sunset, r_presence_in_loop) which add the mechanisms the article lacks. Its 'verifier' block is a checkbox where the store knows three ways verifiers themselves fail (judge crash-masking, judge=generator, unequal arm budgets). Two real gaps in the article: (1) state persists only within a run — no lesson survives to run N+1 or to another repo, the exact gap the OKL exists to fill; (2) zero enforcement — a checklist with no mechanical invoker, the 'surface nobody runs' lesson independently encoded from two repos. Portable use: cite as a decent shared vocabulary for loop design; do not adopt as a method — it has no gates.

[n_a4b40c96ede4] Rule · Hold one arm constant and the experiment measures its own noise floor for free
symptom: an A/B result sits close to its comparison and nobody can say whether the difference is real
fix: keep an arm the change cannot reach, and read its drift between runs as the detection threshold; a between-arm difference smaller than the control's own movement is not a finding
body: cause: the interest-filtering experiment varied only the briefed arm's retrieval, leaving the unaided baseline untouchable by the change. Between two runs hours apart - same tasks, same generator, same judge - that baseline moved 36 to 50 percent. Fourteen points of drift in an arm that could not have changed. The briefed arms differed by one point, so the result is 'no detectable change' with detectable doing real work: this design could not have detected anything smaller than the floor. The report's method section had set its floor at 17 points, the spread of the first four baseline runs; the control measures it again as a by-product of every run, and calibrates every per-task row. The same untouched arm later moved further, and the floor is now at least 21 points (REPORT §4m).

[seed:python-canon:py_docstrings] Rule · Every module, public class and public function has a docstring that lets a reader call it without reading its body
symptom: a public function whose purpose and contract can only be learned by reading its body
fix: select ruff D100-D104 (convention google); write what it is for and what a caller must know
body: PEP 257: all modules, and every function and class a module exports, have docstrings. Google's Python guide sets the bar: 'A docstring should give enough information to write a call to the function without reading the function's code.' One to three lines is usual: what it is for, and what a caller must know - what it returns, what None or an empty filter means, what it raises, a command's exit codes. Writing Args and Returns only where a name and a type do not explain a parameter is a deliberate departure from Google's guide, which lists every parameter. Enforce presence, not format: ruff D100-D104 with pydocstyle convention = "google". Tests can be exempt: a test reads as its name and its comments.

[pretooluse-additionalcontext] Rule · PreToolUse can now add context the model reads, through JSON additionalContext; its plain stdout still cannot
symptom: a design avoids edit-time or tool-time briefing because 'PreToolUse output never reaches the model'
fix: for tool-time context, emit {"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"PreToolUse","additionalContext":"..."}}; keep prompt-time briefing on UserPromptSubmit; re-check the hooks reference before relying on either, since this changed once already
body: cause: okl recorded in 2026-08 that PreToolUse stdout goes to the transcript, not the model, and moved briefings to UserPromptSubmit. Claude Code's hooks reference (checked 2026-10-01) now documents hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext for PreToolUse: wrapped in a system reminder and read on the next model request. Plain stdout reaches the model only for UserPromptSubmit, UserPromptExpansion, SessionStart and PostModelSwitch. SessionStart also fires on compaction (matcher 'compact').

[remote-timeout-not-a-deadline] Defect · A per-socket timeout is not a deadline, and a failure after the request was sent is not 'not written'
symptom: a fail-closed hook against a stalled shared service runs past its host's time limit (Claude Code cancels a UserPromptSubmit hook at 30 s and lets the prompt through unbriefed), or a write reported as lost turns up stored twice after the user retries
fix: budget the caller's worst case per address and per read (or set a real deadline around the whole call), and stop retrying a try that failed slowly, since that is an outage rather than a transient; catch the post-send errors (OSError, http.client.HTTPException) after URLError and fail closed on them; for a write, say 'maybe recorded' (search before retrying, or retry idempotently with the same id), never 'not recorded', and test the retry you call safe: an identical second call must write nothing new, which an append-only history row breaks even when the status write is idempotent (okl #163); keep a test that reads the retry loop's numbers from the shipped hook and asserts the worst case stays under the host's limit
body: cause: Python urllib's timeout applies to each connect attempt, once per address the host resolves to, and to each socket read; it is not a limit on the whole call, and a DNS lookup is not covered at all. urllib wraps connect and send failures in URLError, but failures while reading the reply escape raw: TimeoutError, ConnectionResetError, RemoteDisconnected, BadStatusLine, IncompleteRead. okl's client caught only HTTPError and URLError, so a stalled service crashed okl check with a traceback, and the hook's three 10 s tries took 31.6 s (okl #156, review R10). Two black-holed addresses still took 31.5 s at 5 s a try. Also: bash SECONDS counts whole seconds, so a '-ge N' elapsed check only guarantees a try under N-1 s reads as quick.

[falsifier-relative-to-control] Rule · A pre-registered falsifier is written relative to the control arm measured on the same store, never as an absolute figure
symptom: a pre-registered falsifier fires on the control arm itself, or no cell of a calibration grid can satisfy the selection rule because the baseline already violates it
fix: state every falsifier as a difference from the control arm (the same prompts, the same store, run in the same session), with the allowed size named; when a baseline figure is quoted in the pre-registration, re-measure it on the store the change will run on before writing it; after the fact, apply the rule as written and say so, then report the relative reading beside it rather than quietly substituting the one that passes
body: cause: REPORT §4q (okl, 2026-10-23) pre-registered 'a precision prompt returning twelve records' as a falsifier for a retrieval change. On the live store the full-text control already returned twelve for one prompt, because a lesson recorded since the earlier section matched it, so the absolute clause was unattainable whatever the change did, and the grid written to choose a threshold could satisfy no cell by the rule as stated. The same report's §4p had predicted held-out rows against the probe's own pre-change rows, a different set of sentences, which was also the wrong baseline. Absolute figures and cross-set baselines encode the state of a store that moves; the control arm measured on the same store at the same time is the only baseline the change is responsible against.

[n_041a066035b2] Rule · applies_to stays opt-in: revisit only when off-stack share or framework-bound share roughly doubles
symptom: someone proposes backfilling applies_to across the whole corpus, or asks whether the field is pulling its weight
fix: keep it unset by default and set it only per-record at record time; re-measure the two shares before changing the policy, and never derive the value from a tag
body: cause: measured 2026-09-03 on a 207-record corpus. A python repo's 12 briefing slots were 68 percent untagged/portable, 25 percent off-stack dotnet, 5 percent own-stack, 2 percent off-stack react - and the 32 applies_to-gated records appeared NOWHERE in its ranked candidates, so gating freed zero slots. The off-stack records that do win slots are portable ones (IDOR, pagination caps, rate limiting) that are correctly left unset. Corpus growth alone does not change this: BM25 ranks by match quality, so adding records pushes off-stack ones further down, not up. The scaling risk is the number of distinct STACKS, not corpus size - and its first symptom is redundancy (five stacks each contributing their own pagination rule), which okl dedup addresses, not applicability. Cost asymmetry decides the default: a wrong 'stack-bound' hides a lesson silently, a wrong 'unset' costs one slot of noise. Triggers to revisit: off-stack share of briefings (27 percent at measurement) and framework-bound share of corpus (32/207, 15 percent). Both are queries.

[seed:dotnet-canon:r_encoding_loop] Rule · Encode every 'never again / always when' finding to the smallest surface that catches it — a fix PR without the rule is a half-finished job
symptom: a merged fix for a recurring antipattern with no corresponding rule/gate change
fix: land the rule with the fix (same or paired PR); track deferred encodings as labeled placeholders, never as the encoding itself
body: Findings from any review surface get encoded the same session, into the smallest applicable layer: always-on canon only if every session needs it (keep it lean — size-budgeted in CI), else file-scoped review-bot instructions, a reviewer-agent checklist item, a skill/procedure, or a supporting doc. The fix lives in the PR; the rule lives in the encoding surfaces; the next instance of the antipattern slips through if only the fix lands.

[comparison-table-one-sitting-generated] Rule · A table comparing configurations is a comparison only if one sitting produced every column, and it stays true only if it is generated from those receipts
symptom: a docs or README table of measured figures quotes numbers its cited receipts do not contain, or its columns come from runs at different commits or store sizes, so a difference between columns may be the store and not the setting
fix: re-run every column in one sitting at one commit against one store, print the table from those receipts with a script (okl: evals/standing_table.py), and have the script refuse receipts that disagree on commit or store size; label configurations that differ in more than the setting under comparison (okl: harness versus hook interests)
body: cause: okl #278 (2026-10-24). The evals README's standing table was typed by hand from three receipts: one at commit 1ef28af on a 323-record store and two at b36d1b7 on 322 records, and two of its latencies (24 ms, 538 ms) were from other runs than the receipts it named (18 ms, 492 ms). The review bot caught all three; the author had read each figure from a receipt and still mixed them. A typed figure drifts from its receipt the first time either is regenerated.

[filter-after-fetch-widens-window] Defect · Filtering results after a fixed-size fetch shrinks the window: widen the fetch by what was dropped
symptom: after some records start being excluded (retired, hidden, filtered), a small top-k returns fewer results or none, and the briefing says nothing matched although a live match ranks just below
fix: re-fetch with the window widened by the number excluded (bounded retries), or filter inside the query; test a small limit with excluded records ranked above a live one
body: cause: okl R2 dropped superseded and obsolete lessons after store.search fetched 3x limit; three obsolete matches above a live one left a limit-1 briefing empty, reading 'no encoded rule matched'.

[seed:dotnet-canon:r_pagination_cap] Rule · Every list endpoint paginates with a server-side size cap; keyset pagination for deep offsets
symptom: a list endpoint with no page-size cap, or deep OFFSET pagination on a large table
fix: server-side cap on page size; keyset pagination past shallow offsets
body: An unpaginated list endpoint is an unbounded query a client can weaponize by accident. Cap page size server-side (≤100 here); use keyset (seek) pagination where offsets grow large, since OFFSET N scans N rows to discard them.

[seed:rag-defects:qz_judge_self] Defect · The LLM judge was grading its own homework (same model as the generator)
symptom: the eval's judge model equals (or defaults to) the generator model
fix: require judge≠generator; refuse to run if they're equal
body: The judge defaulted to the same model as the generator — a mirror, not a signal (its default was even an embedding model that can't generate). Portable rule: the judge must be a different model from the generator; refuse to run if they're equal.

[seed:geospatial-defects:d18] Defect · num_classes off-by-one when class 0 is reserved (zero_is_invalid)
symptom: training crashes with 'Target N is out of bounds' where N equals num_classes, or predictions never include the highest class id
body: model.yaml said num_classes: 4; crosswalk emits 4 real classes and class 0 is reserved, so it needs 5. Crashed 'Target 4 is out of bounds'. Contract test: num_classes == max crosswalk id + 1.

[n_a7634ef53a8f] Decision · The encoding loop has no runtime input — every lesson enters from author time or CI time
symptom: a defect class that only a running system reveals (pagination silently dropped, a limit hit under real load, a partial-failure path) has no way into the store until a human finds it some other way
fix: treat observability as a SOURCE of records rather than a competitor to them: when a runtime-only defect is found, record it with found_by naming the trace or metric that showed it; do not claim the loop covers runtime until some record actually cites one
body: cause: measured 2026-09-23 against the corpus. Of the records that state a found_by, the sources are imported canon (CLAUDE.md sections, dated audits), local reproduction (curl against a running service, a scripted agent call), code review, and tests/CI. None cites telemetry from a deployed system. Classified by keyword and then eyeballed, so treat the buckets as indicative rather than exact - but the absence is not marginal, it is total. This matters because the loop's claim is that a lesson paid for once protects every later task, and it is silent about the class of defect that neither a test nor a review can catch. A vendor post (Milan Jovanovic / Dynatrace, brand partnership) makes the same diagnosis from the other side: its Rule 1, give the agent your production standards up front as a skill rather than a prompt, is this project's thesis implemented as the static per-repo rules file the README already positions against; its Rule 2, make checking runtime data a required step, is an input this project does not have. The two compose - observe discovers, okl encodes, the briefing delivers - and reading it as competition would miss that.
